blocks.title: One truth function, several representations
paragraphs: A Boolean function maps each complete input assignment to one output bit. A formula, truth table, sum-of-products and Karnaugh map are different representations of that same mapping.

Keep the variable order explicit. Here A is the most significant input bit. The authored examples use three variables only to make the mathematics inspectable; they do not prescribe the variable count of a future course question.

blocks.title: Evaluate every row before simplifying
paragraphs: Consider F = (A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B). With A fixed at zero, both products are zero. With A fixed at one, one of B and NOT B is one, so F is one. Thus F = A.
In row order AB = 00, 01, 10, 11, the output is 0, 0, 1, 1. Expanding the true rows gives the canonical SoP A·NOT B + A·B; factoring gives A·(NOT B + B) = A.

blocks.title: Construct a sum-of-products
paragraphs: For each required true row, write one product containing every variable: use a variable for input one and its complement for input zero. OR those products. Check that every required one is covered and no required zero is covered.

A shorter SoP may omit variables that change within a valid group. Formula text is not a unique answer: equivalent products can be reordered, and more than one minimum cover can exist. The self-check evaluates the function and the coverage criteria, not one spelling.

blocks.title: Populate a Gray-ordered map
paragraphs: For three inputs, use rows A = 0, 1 and columns BC = 00, 01, 11, 10. The Gray order makes neighboring columns differ in one bit. Copy each truth-table output into its labelled cell, not into ordinary binary column order.
For F = C, the true minterms ABC are 001, 011, 101, 111. Both rows of the map read 0, 1, 1, 0. The two middle columns form a four-cell rectangle.

blocks.title: Group adjacent cells and retain fixed variables
paragraphs: A valid rectangular group contains 1, 2, 4, 8, … cells and spans powers of two in each dimension. Edges wrap: columns 00 and 10 are adjacent because only B changes. Diagonal cells are not adjacent. Every covered cell must be a one or an allowed don’t-care, and all required ones must be covered.

The four-cell group for F = C changes A and B but holds C = 1, so its implicant is C. For NOT C, columns 00 and 10 form a wrapping four-cell group and retain C = 0. Larger valid groups remove more literals; overlapping groups are allowed. Compare complete covers rather than choosing a large group that leaves a one uncovered.

blocks.title: Use don’t-cares only when they help
paragraphs: Suppose required ones are minterms 1 and 3, don’t-cares are 5 and 7, and all other rows must be zero. Without using don’t-cares, a valid term is NOT A·C. Including the two don’t-cares allows the four-cell group C.

Both functions meet every specified row. Don’t-cares need not be covered and are not required ones. C has fewer literals here. In other problems several minimal covers can satisfy the same specified rows; none should be rejected simply for differing from one reference drawing.

blocks.title: Check meaning before appearance
paragraphs: Fix variable order, enumerate the function, populate Gray-labelled cells, then choose legal groups and derive their fixed literals. Verify the result against every specified input.

Practice offers deterministic truth-function and map-population checks, plus unscored SoP/grouping criteria. The Boolean workspace explores truth values; it does not claim to grade arbitrary K-map drawings.

cards.prompt: What must stay fixed when comparing a Boolean formula with a truth table?
cards.answer: The variable identities and row order. Compare the output for every assignment; one differing specified row refutes equivalence.

cards.prompt: How is a minterm formed from one true row?
cards.answer: Include every variable once: uncomplemented for input 1 and complemented for input 0. OR the true-row minterms to obtain canonical SoP.

cards.prompt: Why use BC columns 00, 01, 11, 10 in a K-map?
cards.answer: Successive columns differ in exactly one bit. Ordinary binary order would put 01 next to 10 even though both bits change.

cards.prompt: Must a don’t-care cell be covered?
cards.answer: No. It may be treated as 0 or 1 where helpful, while every specified 1 must be covered and every specified 0 excluded.

cards.prompt: Are the first and last Gray-ordered columns adjacent?
cards.answer: Yes. Map edges wrap when the labels differ in one bit. Diagonal contact alone is not adjacency.

cards.prompt: Which variables survive in the implicant of a group?
cards.answer: Only variables constant across every cell: keep a variable for constant 1 and its complement for constant 0. Variables that change disappear.

cards.prompt: Can two different K-map covers both be valid minima?
cards.answer: Yes. Check legality, coverage, equivalence on specified rows and the stated cost criterion. A different drawing is not automatically wrong.

guided.title: Build and verify a SoP
guided.prompt: Write a SoP for the two-input function whose output rows 00,01,10,11 are 0,1,1,0.
rubric: Canonical SoP is NOT A·B + A·NOT B. Equivalent ordering is allowed.
Check all four rows. A+B is wrong because it includes 11.
The workspace does not parse or automatically score arbitrary formula text.

guided.title: Compare valid grouping choices
guided.prompt: Use the three-variable Gray layout from Learn. Required ones: 1,3; don’t-cares: 5,7; all others zero. Explain two valid covers and why one has fewer literals.
rubric: NOT A·C covers exactly the required ones; C also includes allowed don’t-cares.
C is the four-cell group at columns 01 and 11, across both A rows, and uses one literal.
Check rectangular power-of-two groups, wrap rules and specified zero exclusion. Multiple valid answers are accepted through self-check, not numeric grading.
